record.paper_title: Observational properties of diffuse radio sources in Galaxy Clusters: Current knowledge and open questions
record.original_question: Which galaxy clusters contain both a firmly detected shock front and a radio relic with a clear spatial and physical connection, and does a larger sample of such systems support the view that relics are produced by merger-driven shocks with Mach numbers less than or approximately equal to 3?

evidence.quote: The location, shape and polarization properties of relics suggest that their origin is connected to the propagation of shock waves, with Mach numbers <∼3, during cluster mergers.

For a few well studied cases, the spectrum of the radio halo is consistent with Mach numbers for the shock in the range 1–3 (i.e. A 521, Giacintucci et al. 2008; CIZA J2242.8+5301, van Weeren et al. 2010; A 754, Macario et al. 2011).

So far only a few shocks have been ﬁrmly detected with Chandra (Markevitch et al., present volume), and it would be crucial to increase the statistics not only of conﬁrmed shocks, but also of clusters with a clear connection between a shock front and a relic, as it has been the case for A 520 (Markevitch et al. 2005) and A 754 (Macario et al. 2011).

artifact.self_contained_problem:
In the intracluster medium of merging galaxy clusters, two observational signatures are of interest: (i) shock fronts, defined as surfaces across which the X-ray surface brightness and gas temperature exhibit discontinuities consistent with the Rankine–Hugoniot jump conditions for a Mach number M > 1, as detected with high-resolution X-ray imaging; and (ii) radio relics, defined as elongated, often peripheral, polarized regions of diffuse synchrotron emission with steep radio spectra and Mpc-scale extent. A "clear spatial and physical connection" between a shock front and a radio relic means that the X-ray-detected shock surface coincides spatially with the outer edge of the relic and that the Mach number inferred independently from the X-ray jump is consistent with the Mach number inferred from the relic's integrated radio spectral index under the diffusive shock acceleration relation M^2 = (2α − 3)/(2α + 1), where α is the integrated spectral index of the relic.

Identify the set S of galaxy clusters for which both a shock front (in the above sense) is firmly detected and a radio relic with such a clear spatial and physical connection to that shock front has been observed. Determine, for the clusters in S, the empirical distribution of Mach numbers, and decide whether this distribution supports the hypothesis that radio relics are produced by merger-driven shocks with Mach numbers M ≲ 3.
artifact.category_tag: Galaxy cluster radio relics and merger shocks
artifact.status_search_result: Subsequent observational and simulation work has expanded the catalog of clusters where X-ray–detected shock fronts coincide with radio relics (e.g., A520, A754, CIZA J2242.8+5301, the Sausage and Toothbrush relics, A2744, A3667, etc.), and the inferred X-ray Mach numbers are typically in the range 1.5–3, broadly consistent with the M ≲ 3 hypothesis. However, a persistent discrepancy exists in which radio-derived Mach numbers tend to exceed X-ray-derived ones, and recent simulation studies (e.g., TNG-Cluster, 2024) describe shock surfaces as composites with broad Mach distributions peaking at 2–4.5. The qualitative picture of low-Mach merger shocks producing relics is supported, but the underlying acceleration mechanism and Mach-number tension remain unresolved.

status_evidence.title: Radio relics in massive galaxy cluster mergers in the TNG-Cluster simulation
status_evidence.snippet: Independent detections of shock fronts from X-ray observations across radio relics further support the merger shock-radio relic connection.
status_evidence.claim: More clusters now have firmly detected shock fronts coincident with radio relics, supporting the merger-shock origin.

status_evidence.title: Morphology and Mach Number Distribution of Merger Shock Surfaces in Merging Galaxy Clusters
status_evidence.snippet: The distribution of Mach numbers of shock zones on each surface can be approximated by a log-normal function, peaking at approximately 2-4.5.
status_evidence.claim: Simulated merger shock Mach number distributions peak at low values consistent with M ≲ a few, though tails extend higher.

status_evidence.title: Can cluster merger shocks reproduce the luminosity and shape distribution of radio relics?
status_evidence.snippet: Mach numbers obtained from radio observations are larger than the corresponding X-ray measurements.
status_evidence.claim: A systematic radio-vs-X-ray Mach number discrepancy persists, leaving the diffusive shock acceleration interpretation only partially confirmed.
